cues.txt: [ANNOUNCER] Session.
It is my pleasure to introduce our first conversation with
Dean Sarah Soule and former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak.
(applause)
[ANNOUNCER] Sarah A. Soule is the Philip H. Knight Professor and Dean
at Stanford Graduate School of Business.
She is also the Morgridge Professor of
Organizational Behavior.
Her major areas of interest are organizational theory,
social movements, and political sociology.
Rishi Sunak is Member of Parliament for Richmond and
Northallerton in the United Kingdom, and is the William C.
Edwards Distinguished Visiting Fellow at the
Hoover Institution.
You've heard of him, of course, because he was Chancellor
of the Exchequer and then Prime Minister of the
UK from 2022 to 2024.
In those leadership roles, he made key policy decisions on
a wide range of technological, medical, economic,
and geopolitical issues.
Importantly for us, he earned his MBA
here at the GSB.
One final note before we begin.
A few weeks ago, Rishi had a skiing accident,
and his recovery from that accident has prevented him
from being able to travel to California for this event.
So Rishi will be joining us on screen rather than in person.
Please join me in welcoming Dean Soule and Rishi.
(applause)
[SARAH SOULE] Thank you, Ken.
Thank you for that wonderful welcome and
wonderful introduction.
I am so delighted to see all of you here,
and I can't think of a better person to help
us kick off the forum than Rishi Sunak, who,
as many of you know from the introduction and from
his biography, is probably one of the world's greatest
experts on navigating very complicated contextual factors.
So let us begin.
Rishi, thank you so much for joining us.
We're so delighted that you're here with us today.
And there's so much going on in the world right now,
and your perspective is going to allow us to kick off the
conversation with great style
And I think great intellectual discussion.
So I'll dive in with my first question.
Let's talk a little bit about the international order.
Often we hear people say that the international
order is being renegotiated in real time right now.
Some people say, of course, that the order that we have built up
over decades is gone for good.
Others say that we're more in a period of renegotiation
I'd like to ask you from where you sit, what does this seem,
what is this like to you, Rishi?
[RISHI SUNAK] Well, first of all, good morning, Sarah.
Good morning, everyone.
Thank you for having me, and my apologies again that
I can't be with you in person.
As you heard from Ken, I was skiing a couple of—
Weeks ago.
And I guess to put it in GSB terms, my BHAG for my
ski trip was to prove to my two teenage daughters that
their daddy was still the best skier in the family.
But it turned out for a 45-year-old, that was too big,
too hairy, too audacious a goal to succeed in.
So I attempted to jump
on the last day to put them right and
I've ended up on the no-fly zone list.
So apologies for that.
But to go to your question,
what I can say is,
whilst I'm in bad shape and
hopefully I'll be back skiing again,
that's certainly not the case for the international
rules-based order that we all grew up with and got used to.
And I think that the
tricky thing is for
leaders especially is just accepting that reality,
right?
We shouldn't spend time debating whether that's a good thing,
whether it's a bad thing.
We just have to accept that
that is the new reality.
The tricky thing is also, though,
we don't know what's replaced it.
It's not as if we've gone from one particular set of rules
and an operating framework to a clear alternative.
We're in this period of transition,
and what history tells us is that
those periods of transition,
can be quite unpredictable and actually quite bloody.
I think it's not a coincidence
that right now there's more conflict around the world than
at any point since World War II.
But what I can say is I think some of the features
of this new world order are starting to take shape
I mean, the first is that
stability as we got used to
is gone.
We have to get used to a more unpredictable environment.
Pax Americana, as we knew it,
is clearly not operating and
going to operate in the same way,
partly because the US is
redefining its role in the
world under this administration,
but some of those forces were in place before.
But also because, for the first time
in its modern history, in China,
the US has a clear peer competitor
across economic, military, and technology domains.
You contrast that to the Soviet Union, though.
China is far more integrated into the global economy.
Many more countries trade far more with China than they do
with the US, so that injects a degree of complexity.
Then alongside that, you've got the rise of
global swing states, as they've been called,
countries like India, which don't neatly
fit into any box.
They're going to kind of go their own way,
and we have to adjust to that.
We've got a kind of increasing
I guess cooperation between countries like Iran, Russia,
North Korea, and China, which causes its own challenges,
particularly for those of us in Europe.
And you put all of that together, as I said,
we've got a quite unpredictable situation.
And I guess the key takeaway for me is
not just adjusting to this new world,
but adjusting to it means recognizing that
hard power matters again.
And I think for a generation of leaders
that were operating in a different framework,
which you described, Sarah,
the kind of new realization is, hard power is back, it matters,
and you need to invest in it if you are a country.
[SARAH SOULE] Okay, thank you.
Thank you, Rishi.
Let's talk a little bit about the special relationship between
the United States and the UK.
How important do you think of this alliance and other
such alliances as we think about the New World Order?
[RISHI SUNAK] Yeah, it, um, it...
Obviously, people like myself
and many, many Brits are firm believers that
the US and the transatlantic alliance, first of all,
between the UK and the US,
Europe and the US, is incredibly important,
not just to European security and prosperity,
but to global security and prosperity.
I firmly believe that;
that I have always advocated for it.
I think an active US around the world is a force for good.
And the US has always been, in my view and many others,
a very benign hegemon with an
enlightened view of its own self-interest.
Now, what's happened over the last several months
has put a lot of pressure on
On that set of beliefs.
And I think that's particularly challenging for those like
myself in Europe who are such strong supporters of
the special relationship of the Transatlantic Alliance, not
least because it has allowed our French friends to say, you know,
"We told you so,"
which is never a fun thing for a Brit.
But look, I was very fortunate personally
to have a strong relationship with Joe, with President Biden.
We had a fortuitous
Calendar, which meant we saw each other almost every month
for a period of six months during our terms in office,
which is quite rare actually amongst these relationships
between leaders.
You know, the personalities do make a difference, and we
had the opportunity to build a good personal connection,
and we enjoyed each other's company, and that certainly
helped get things done.
But having said that, you know, when I went
through, particularly with our intelligence
and defense senior officials
And advisors, you know, what was very clear to me
is, you know, that personal relationship kind of sits at
the top of a very deep pyramid.
And there's so much operational,
on-the-ground
historical cooperation that is happening
that the relationship can survive, you know, the
ups and downs between any
Two individuals, and there have been many
times throughout history where
you've had personality clashes
or slight misalignment of views.
But it is a relationship that has endured because
it is deep, particularly at that intelligence,
military, and security level.
And we share the same values and have stood together to fight,
whether it's the forces of communism and fascism at
points in our history.
And I'm confident that the two countries will remain close.
And if you put it this way, just think about it:
you know, your country, America, is celebrating 250 years of
independence this year.
And one of the ways that the US has chosen to celebrate
kind of unshackling itself from
Britain is to invite the-
Great, great, great, great, great, great, great, great
grandson of George III
over for a historic state visit
and address to Congress.
So I think that tells us that the special
relationship will endure.
[SARAH SOULE] Very nicely said.
Thank you so much.
And let's shift gears a little bit to think a little bit about
generally about Europe
and kind of the sort of
stubbornly elusive growth in the region.
What is your honest diagnosis?
Is it a policy problem?
Is this a structural problem,
or is it something else?
[RISHI SUNAK] Yeah, the first thing, and particularly, you know, for
when I'm talking to our American colleagues and friends,
and indeed actually my European peers, is for us to be really
honest about the challenge.
And by challenge I mean the gap that has opened up between
the US and Europe when it comes to economic growth in a
relatively short space of time.
If you go back maybe just a decade or so,
Europe and the US had pretty similar-sized economies.
Fast-forward not that long,
10 years, 12 years, and the US has outperformed by about
a third, which is actually, if you think about it, pretty
extraordinary outperformance in a short space of time.
Another way to think about it,
which is quite striking, is if
you think about GDP per capita, which I appreciate is not a
perfect measure of prosperity, but it's a pretty decent one.
If Europe was a state, if Europe was an American state,
on a GDP per capita basis, it would be the poorest
state in America.
And not just by a little bit, by about $10,000 per head.
So that is the scale of the gap that we're talking about.
And so look, we have to recognize
that something is not working as any of us
would want it to be.
And it needs addressing.
Now, actually, my friend and former colleague,
Mario Draghi, who's written, as everyone knows, a very
comprehensive report,
I think where people are actually pretty supportive
in theory of all the things that Mario has said in that
enormous report about how to restore
European growth and competitiveness.
The reality is, Sarah, to answer your question.
I think at last count, 10% or so
of Mario's recommendations
had been adopted, and we're
a few years on now.
So there clearly is work to do.
Partly the challenge is, and Ken alluded to it right
at the beginning, is, you know,
politics and leadership isn't easy.
And, and...
Jean-Claude Juncker,
who was a European Commission
president from before,
I think maybe summarized it
best when he said,
"We know exactly what to do.
We just don't know how to get
elected again once we've done it."
And hopefully we can rise
to the challenge in Europe,
but that's a little bit where we are.
[SARAH SOULE] Okay.
It's a little bit like academic administration,
I think, in some sense.
All right, I want to shift gears
just a little bit, too.
Part of the theme today, of course, will be technology
and rapidly shifting technology and AI.
And so I want to think a little bit about that and
ask you a question.
Amidst all of the geopolitical change that we've touched a bit
on, we're in, of course, another technology revolution.
And I've heard you describe this as a paradox for leaders.
Can you share a little bit more about what you mean by this,
by this phrase, paradox for leaders,
when talking about this?
[RISHI SUNAK] Yeah, I think actually goes back to probably
your opening question.
And this geopolitical world
that we're living in, I think genuinely is
the most dangerous period of our adult lifetimes.
And I said that in a speech when I announced an increase
to UK defence spending, and I was with the NATO
Secretary General at the time, and we were in Poland,
and this is a few years ago, talking about this new
geopolitical world and the need for us to invest
more and rise to meet the threats that we've faced.
But the paradox, as you put it,
and what I said in the
same speech, is as though the paradox of the moment.
Is that it's at the same time the most transformational
time that any of us have ever lived in.
And that is of course, because of AI.
Not exclusively because of AI, but predominantly,
and that's because AI is a general-purpose technology,
and these don't come along all that often, right?
We're very lucky as policymakers,
as practitioners
To be living at a time where this technology has come along,
which has, like steam power and electricity before it,
the opportunity to transform every aspect of
our lives, our economies,
and our societies if we harness it correctly.
And I think it's incumbent on us as leaders,
not to listen to the first dialogue exchange
that you and I had about all the difficult geopolitics
and dive back under your duvet and not come out.
You need to equally say, "Hang on.
We're living through this incredible moment,
and I have the ability, I have agency to shape our
destiny," whether it's as an organization, as a country.
And grasp this thing, learn the lessons
from history about how best to do that.
But actually, if we properly harness this thing,
I think we can deliver an enormous amount of
prosperity and indeed more security to our citizens.
So that's the paradox, as I said, of the moment.
You've got both of these things coexisting at the same time.
[SARAH SOULE] That's great. And so what I'm hearing you say
is that this is really
about spreading and deploying the technology effectively,
responsibly, and principally.
Can you elaborate a little bit on what that might
look like in practice?
[RISHI SUNAK] Yeah.
And I think you hit on an
incredibly important distinction,
because often when people instinctively talk about
how do you win in AI or who's winning the AI race, you know,
your mind, and certainly the media headlines are
drawn to this race for AGI, for super intelligence.
I'm sure some of the people sitting in the audience are
working on it themselves, right?
And in this race, who's going to get
there first?
Is it the US?
Is it China?
Which lab is ahead this week on which benchmark?
Um...
Now, whilst that's certainly important,
and as someone who believes deeply in Western
liberal values prevailing, I very much want
the US labs to win, and I think it's
important that they do.
But I think the kind of more interesting race is
the race you described.
It's the race for what I call everyday AI.
Who can spread the benefit of this technology across their
country for the benefit of their citizens as quickly
and as broadly as possible?
And that I think is the thing that we as policymakers need
to focus more on and maybe doesn't get enough attention.
And history, I think, here is instructive because
history tells us something.
And actually, I feel like I
learnt this in a book that Brad Smith from
Microsoft had given to me when I left office.
And one of the great advantages of leaving a
job like being Prime Minister is you have time to think.
And I'm sure like all people in these big leadership jobs
will say the same thing, but carving out time to
think when you're in those jobs is, is enormously difficult,
and the urgent always crowds out the important.
But anyway, Brad had given me this book by a professor
called Jeffrey Ding, who wrote this book called
Technology and Great Powers,
Technology Diffusion of Great Powers,
and it talks about
This throughout history.
And the kind of example,
Well, his key point is—the key takeaway is, look,
you don't need to be the country that invents the technology
to be the country that benefits from it the most, right?
So if we're not Silicon Valley,
if we're not Beijing, that's okay.
We should take heart from that.
And the example he gives, which I love,
so forgive me for spending a second on it
because I think it's instructive,
is you go all the way.
This pattern has repeated throughout history.
You can go all the way back to the Middle Ages and
the printing press, which was a really seminal technological
innovation of its time.
It happened in Germany in a town called Mainz.
But it wasn't Germany that got the benefit of
inventing the printing press, it was actually the Dutch.
And when you kind of go and look up,
well, why was that?
There are a few interesting things that emerge.
The first was that the Dutch didn't have the
same censorship laws that Germany had.
They were much more open about people being able to write
and say what they wanted.
And so that obviously was a great boon for
those in the business of publishing the written word.
The second thing was they didn't have the
same history of guilds or unions that Germany had.
What those guilds served to do was essentially
really tightly control who was allowed to set up a
printing organization or a printing press.
You know, it's kind of like state licensing, which we
do a lot of work on at Stanford, and the impact
of those restrictions.
And then the third thing, which I found interesting
with a background in finance, is the much more developed
capital markets in Amsterdam
meant that those involved in
the printing business could much more easily hedge
their paper costs, which were pretty volatile.
And so you had these three
Kind of related institutional developments, none of which had
anything to do with the printing press itself, but they allowed
the Dutch to become not just the publishing powerhouses
of Europe, but of the world.
And Erik Brynjolfsson, again, you know,
of our parish here, has spoken a lot about this.
And it's figuring out what are the equivalents of those things
that I just outlined today that will allow leaders to get the
benefit of this technology for their organization,
for their country?
What does that diffusion infrastructure
architecture look like?
And we can get into that, but that's the
kind of the thesis, and I think that's
where people need to focus more attention.
[SARAH SOULE] Yeah. That's such a great example,
and it's a perfect example
for kicking off the Stanford Leadership Institute,
because, of course,
this is part of what we are really going to be
grappling with these sort of multi-layered,
very, very sort of complicated context
in which any kind of decision is made,
and understanding all of those pieces at once
is really what we are going to be about at this institute.
So I'm really glad you took a little time to take that detour
and to give us that wonderful example.
Let me follow up, though, with a question because
it leads to the obvious possibly next question,
which is about regulation of AI.
Maybe you could say a little bit
about where you stand on this
and what you think it means to
actually get that right
from a governmental perspective.
[RISHI SUNAK] Yeah.
This is one of these
great things that you have to grapple with
when you're in these jobs.
I'm someone who's a free market-
Conservative by instinct and tradition, and generally
believe that's the right approach for creating growth,
for creating opportunities, spreading prosperity.
Now, you know, of course, there are always sensible
reasons to regulate whether there are market failures
and other things, or something else that we think
the market won't protect that we value, and that
your job in these policy roles is to try and
figure out that balance and get it right
And obviously AI was something that happened,
or at least thinking about it
happened while I was in the office.
And I was really struck by a
meeting I had in Downing Street
in 2022 when Dario
founded Anthropic,
Sam from OpenAI,
and Demis from DeepMind
all came to see me.
And we sat, and they wanted to
talk to me about what they were seeing.
And the fact that they had come together was in and
itself a big thing.
There wasn't that many things that
I think at that point they had done together.
But they were keen to come together and talk to
me a little bit about the pace of the development,
and that was what they wanted to impress upon me,
was that this thing that all of them in different ways had
been working on for a long time was really beginning
to scale in a way that was surprising even then.
And they thought people
like me needed to be informed about that,
to be thinking about what that meant.
And we ended up having a very
Long series of thoughtful discussions thereafter,
which culminated in the Leaders' Summit on AI,
which I hosted at Bletchley Park.
And I'm really pleased that that
summit series was a success.
And the idea was, look,
this is this new thing
that's come along,
which is going to be
so transformational.
That it requires leaders to be able to come together and
discuss it in a dedicated forum, not just as a kind of panel
discussion at a G7 or a G20, but it needs its own forum.
And slightly differently to things like the G7 and the G20,
because this development is
happening largely in the private sector,
I thought it was important that we brought
the technology entrepreneurs and developers together
with the leaders in a forum.
And then we did that at Bletchley,
and subsequently that summit's been held
in France, in South Korea, and India.
Just a few months ago.
And so there now at least is a forum to discuss these issues.
So what's the right approach?
I tend to come down on the side of the argument that
says we are too early in this for there to be very heavy
top-down legislation of AI.
The technology is changing far faster than most governments
and legislators can put laws in place,
And that doesn't strike me as a recipe for success.
Given we talked earlier about the challenges that Europe in
particular has with growth.
Innovation is a big opportunity to provide some growth,
and so stifling this at birth, you know, again,
doesn't strike me as being the right thing to do.
So I took the decision that there shouldn't be
top-down new legislation, regulation on AI in the UK.
That was a different decision to the decision that the EU took.
They put in place the EU AI Act, which actually Mario, who
we were talking about earlier, has subsequently said should
be paused and rolled back, which is now happening.
So I think they are recognizing.
That maybe wasn't the
right approach as well.
You know, that said, that doesn't mean that
I think we should do nothing.
And I think if you're sitting in these jobs,
your first duty always is the safety and security of
your citizens that you're very privileged to represent, right?
At the end of the day, that is your responsibility,
and it rests solely with you.
And something that's come along that the people developing the
technology themselves have been very open with you
about the potential risks, like all new technologies
provide for bad actors.
For malicious use and then potentially more autonomous
activity down the line.
So, you know, the theme of our first summit in Bletchley was
on this topic of AI security.
And my approach then was to say what we need is
to develop the technical expertise in government.
So we created the AI Security Institute in the UK.
We funded it well.
It's independent of government in a sense.
It's not a regulator.
And its mission is to work actually constructively
with the labs to evaluate these models before they
are released to the public, to identify potential risks
in the areas of cyber.
Bio, and obviously nuclear
and other threats as well.
So in these very significant national security risks,
accepting that this technology is developing,
there's a handful of very large models that
potentially pose new risks.
We should have the capability and the expertise to evaluate
them so that we know at some point if there's a reason for us
to do more, then we can do that.
So we've reached an agreement with the labs to do that,
And I'm really pleased to say
that that has worked really well.
And it's a model that other countries have worked
with the UK on.
The labs have constructively, proactively provided the models.
And you've seen recently, obviously.
Some discussion in the news
about a new set of models
posing some new cyber risks.
Important we get ahead of those.
And so I think that is the right
template for now.
Look, that might change.
It's something that we will have
to constantly keep under review.
But what I say is
a couple of things.
If you're in a country like the UK,
you have to accept
there's very little you can
do about this on your own
at the end of the day. Right,
the US, given that these are
largely US companies,
will need to decide how
it wants to do this.
It is focused on the race
with China, which is important,
and they-- we can't let China--
Get ahead in that regard.
So that is a tricky dynamic.
But the thing, maybe I'll leave it here.
Sorry for the long answer.
Is why someone who
believes firmly in being pro-innovation, pro-growth,
thinks that technology is an enormous force for good.
The reason we still have to think a little bit carefully
about this is because we have to win the battle for trust
in the eyes of the public.
And obviously, I'm virtually with you.
We're sitting in Silicon Valley.
We don't need convincing that technology is an
incredible force for good.
But actually, the vast majority
of our citizens in places like the US,
the UK, and others, their overwhelming feeling
about AI is one of fear.
It's one of pessimism.
And we need to change that if we want to capture all
the benefits from it, because ultimately people
are not going to adopt a technology that they're
scared or fearful of.
And part of our ability to win that battle for trust is
going to be persuading them and showing them that we're on
top of any risks that AI might bring and we can handle them.
So I think actually, being responsible about
AI security is just the other side of the coin of
ensuring that we can get all the benefits from it as well.
[SARAH SOULE] Mm-hmm. That's terrific.
And yes, I know that at least what I have noticed
here on campus in the last couple of years is a real,
what feels like a move from fear
To a move to a genuine excitement and engagement.
And I also recognize that at Stanford and Silicon Valley,
we're in a bit of a bubble on that with respect to AI.
Oh, so very, very well said, and a good reminder that
we can't let our view of this be clouded by the
space that we are in right now.
Your mention of trust, I think, is really important,
and it reminds me of-
It's the first time that we met last summer, and we had a long
conversation about leadership and what it meant to you to
be a GSB-trained leader.
And I want to come back to something we talked a
little bit then about then.
And we talked a little bit about your experience leading
during the pandemic, of course, and the kind of uncertainty
that we all experienced.
And we, I think, most of us had a lot of empathy for those
like yourself who were in governmental
positions at that time,
and the weight of the decisions
that you were taking every single day.
And I'm hoping I can ask you to just reflect for the audience
on what surprised you about yourself as a leader during
that incredibly uncertain time?
[RISHI SUNAK] Yeah, it...
Yeah, well, I became Chancellor
in February 2020.
And at the time, it was pretty-
[SARAH SOULE] Good timing.
[RISHI SUNAK] Yeah.
Well...
The funny thing was,
at the time, it was
very much a battlefield promotion,
one might describe it as.
Which was good training for when
I became Prime Minister
as well, it turned out.
But I had inherited a Budget Day,
From my predecessor, and so I got this job.
But I had to deliver a budget for the UK,
which we do annually here, and you would've seen it on telly,
maybe the Chancellor standing outside Downing Street with
the red box and all of that.
But I had to deliver that budget for the country in
three and a half weeks, I think.
And I thought when I got the job,
"Wow, doing this budget is going to be the hardest"
thing I will ever have to do."
But then obviously, COVID struck, and it
turned out delivering that budget was the easiest
thing I had to do for the next two and a half years.
And thinking back,
what did I learn?
There's a moment that stood out for me very early.
I remember I was very young.
I wasn't 40 yet at the time.
I was 39,
and I'd gone from having the most junior job in the cabinet.
We don't have a designated survivor equivalent in the UK.
But if there was, that was my job
in the cabinet beforehand.
I'd gone from having that job to
having this kind of second most
important job after the prime minister.
And then this pandemic struck,
and the thing that really struck me
in the first kind of week of it.
We had a failed gilt auction,
and there'll be lots of economists in the room.
And I was like, I don't think
my debt markets class at the GSB,
Darrell Duffie, I don't think covered that
when I was there.
And that hadn't happened in a very long time.
And just obviously, for the non-economists or
finance people in the room,
it's the government selling
its debt, and then you do that all the time.
Normally, it's totally fine.
But we had a failed auction,
so that we didn't sell all the
debt that we assumed we would be able to.
That's kind of a once-in-a-very- long-time-type occurrence.
And that was a moment of extreme anxiety for me.
Here I was, 39 years old, I just got this thing.
We're in this... No one had dealt with a pandemic before,
so I had to figure all that out.
And then you're faced with the prospect that
the country, the government, you know, can't fund itself.
Obviously it was fine and we could, but I
ended up having to negotiate something called the
Ways and Means Facility with the Bank of England,
which is a fancy name for an overdraft, it turns out.
Which is, if we can't finance ourselves, I can
basically ask the Bank of England to do an overdraft.
We didn't end up needing it, but it was
a precautionary measure.
